title: Three Parts, Twenty-Four Books, One Scroll
bigQuestion: How did the Tanakh get its shape, and how has its text been kept the same for so long?

story.title: One Letter Wrong
story.kicker: A scribe leans over a sheet of parchment and counts, because a single wrong letter can undo a whole column of work.
paragraphs: The room is quiet. A man sits at a slanted desk with a sheet of parchment in front of him. In his hand is a quill cut from a feather. Beside him is a pot of black ink. He is a *sofer*, a scribe. He is writing a Torah scroll, and he has been at it for almost a year.

He does not write from memory. Jewish law says a scribe must copy from another correct text, letter by letter. Before he writes the name of God, he says out loud that he is writing it for its holiness. He checks each word against his model. Then he writes it. Then he checks it again.

Now he stops. Something is wrong. Two letters in the last line look too close together. He holds the sheet up to the light. The letters must not touch. If they touch, the scroll is not fit to be read from. He scrapes the ink away with a blade and writes the letters again, a little farther apart.

This is slow work. A finished Torah scroll has 304,805 letters, as Jewish tradition counts them. Every one has to be right. When the scribe is done, a checker will go over the whole scroll. Today some checkers use a computer to scan the columns and flag any letter that looks off.

Why so much care? Jewish tradition treats the words of the Torah as holy, and the exact letters matter. Historians see something else too. This care is one reason the text of the Tanakh has changed so little over more than a thousand years. In this chapter you will learn how the book got its shape, what languages it uses, and who kept its text.
story.think: Why might a community decide that a scroll with one wrong letter cannot be used? What would be lost if scribes were less careful?

lessons.title: Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim
lessons.mainIdea: The Tanakh is three collections in one book: Torah (Teaching), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings), twenty-four books in all.
reading: The word *Tanakh* is made from three Hebrew letters: T, N and K. Each one stands for a part of the book. T is for *Torah*, which means teaching. N is for *Nevi'im*, the Prophets. K is for *Ketuvim*, the Writings. Say the three letters together and you get Tanakh.

The Torah has five books. In Hebrew they are named for their first words: Bereshit, Shemot, Vayikra, Bamidbar and Devarim. In English they are Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. Jewish tradition holds the Torah as the heart of the whole book. It is the part read from a scroll every week in the synagogue.

The Prophets come next. Jewish tradition splits them in two. The Former Prophets tell a story: Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings. The Latter Prophets hold the words of prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve. The Twelve short books count as one book in the Tanakh.

The Writings come last. They are a mixed shelf: Psalms, Proverbs, Job, the five short scrolls, Daniel, Ezra-Nehemiah and Chronicles. Counted the Jewish way, with Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra-Nehemiah and the Twelve each as one book, the whole Tanakh has twenty-four books.

words.d: the Hebrew Bible; the name is made from the first letters of its three parts, Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim
teaching; the first five books of the Tanakh, from Genesis to Deuteronomy
the Prophets; the second part of the Tanakh, from Joshua to the Twelve
the Writings; the third part of the Tanakh, from Psalms to Chronicles

look.title: Books in Each Part of the Tanakh

look.prompt: The Prophets part has eight books but takes up many pages. Which of its books do you think hold more than one short book inside?

check.q: What do the three letters of the word Tanakh stand for?
choices: Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim
Talmud, Nevi'im, Kohanim
Torah, Nehemiah, Kings
Tehillim, Nevi'im, Ketuvim
check.why: Tanakh is an acronym: T for Torah (Teaching), N for Nevi'im (Prophets), K for Ketuvim (Writings).

check.q: Which part of the Tanakh is read from a scroll each week in the synagogue?
choices: The Writings
The Torah
The Twelve
Chronicles
check.why: The five books of the Torah are read in a yearly cycle from a handwritten scroll; the other parts are read from printed books or chanted at special times.

check.q: How many books does the Tanakh have when counted the traditional Jewish way?
check.why: Jewish tradition counts 24 books, treating Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra-Nehemiah and the Twelve as one book each. Protestant Bibles count the same texts as 39.

lessons.title: Two Orders, Two Endings
lessons.mainIdea: Christians read the same books in a different order and count them differently, so the Old Testament ends with Malachi while the Tanakh ends with Chronicles.
reading: The books Christians call the Old Testament are the same books as the Tanakh. But the order is not the same. Protestant Bibles put the books in four groups: law, history, poetry and prophets. So Chronicles sits near the front with the history books, and the prophets come last. The last book is Malachi.

The Tanakh keeps Chronicles at the very end of the Writings. Its last verse is a call from the Persian king Cyrus to the exiles: let anyone who belongs to God's people go up to Jerusalem. So the Tanakh closes with a return home. Jewish readers have often noticed that the book ends on a journey that is about to begin.

The count differs too. Protestant Bibles list 39 books. They split Samuel, Kings and Chronicles into two books each. They split Ezra from Nehemiah. They count each of the Twelve prophets as its own book. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles add other books, such as Maccabees and Sirach, that the Tanakh does not include.

Historians explain the difference by history. Early Christians mostly read the Bible in a Greek translation called the *Septuagint*, and its order became the Christian order. Jewish communities kept the three-part Hebrew order. Neither order is more correct. They are two ways of arranging the same shelf.

words.d: the Christian name for the books of the Tanakh, arranged in a different order and often counted as 39 books
an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun around the 3rd century BCE, whose order shaped the Christian Old Testament
the last book of the Tanakh; it retells the story of Israel and ends with a call to go up to Jerusalem

look.title: The Last Words of the Tanakh
look.text: The Tanakh ends with a message from Cyrus, king of Persia. He says that the LORD has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and has charged him to build a house in Jerusalem. Then he says: whoever among you belongs to God's people, may God be with him, and let him go up.
look.cite: 2 Chronicles 36:23, paraphrased from the JPS Tanakh (1917)
look.prompt: Compare this ending with the last verse of Malachi in a Christian Bible, which warns of a coming day of judgment. What feeling does each ending leave with a reader?

check.q: Which book comes last in the Tanakh?
choices: Malachi
Nehemiah
Deuteronomy
Chronicles
check.why: The Tanakh ends with 2 Chronicles and Cyrus's call to go up to Jerusalem. Malachi is the last book of the Christian Old Testament.

check.q: Why do Protestant Bibles count 39 books where the Tanakh counts 24?
choices: They split books like Samuel and Kings in two and count each of the Twelve prophets separately
They add the Talmud as fifteen extra books
They leave out the Writings
They count each psalm as a book
check.why: The texts are the same; the difference is in splitting Samuel, Kings, Chronicles and Ezra-Nehemiah and counting the Twelve as twelve books.

check.q: According to historians, what shaped the Christian order of the Old Testament?
choices: A vote at the Council of Nicaea
The order of the Greek Septuagint
The order Rashi chose
The Dead Sea Scrolls
check.why: Early Christians mostly read the Greek Septuagint, whose grouping into law, history, poetry and prophets became the Christian order.

lessons.title: How the Canon Settled
lessons.mainIdea: The Tanakh's list of books, its canon, formed in stages: Torah first, then Prophets, then Writings, and tradition remembers the rabbis at Yavneh discussing the last books.
reading: A *canon* is a list of the books a community holds as its scripture. The Tanakh's canon did not appear all at once. Scholars and Jewish tradition agree that the Torah was accepted first. The book of Nehemiah tells of Ezra reading the Torah aloud to the whole people in Jerusalem, around the 5th century BCE.

The Prophets were gathered next. By about 200 BCE, Jewish writers were already speaking of "the Law and the Prophets" as a set. The Writings took longest. Books like Esther, Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs were still being discussed by the rabbis in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE.

Jewish tradition remembers rabbis meeting at *Yavneh*, a town near the coast, after the Temple fell in 70 CE. The Mishnah records their debates about whether certain books "make the hands unclean," a phrase for holy books. Older scholars spoke of a council at Yavneh that closed the canon. Most scholars today think the process was slower and less formal.

What the debates show is that the community was asking careful questions. Which books belong? Which were written under prophecy, as the rabbis put it? By the 2nd century CE the list of twenty-four was settled, and it has not changed since.

words.d: the official list of books a community counts as its scripture
a town where rabbis gathered after 70 CE; tradition links their discussions to the last books of the canon
the first written collection of rabbinic law and discussion, edited around 200 CE

look.title: A Debate About Song of Songs
look.text: The Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5) records rabbis discussing whether Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes "make the hands unclean," the rabbis' way of saying a book is holy scripture. Rabbi Akiva is remembered as saying that no one in Israel ever disputed Song of Songs, and that all the Writings are holy, but Song of Songs is the holy of holies.
look.prompt: Song of Songs is a love poem that never names God. Why might some rabbis have questioned it, and why might Rabbi Akiva have defended it so strongly?

check.q: Which part of the Tanakh was accepted as scripture first?
choices: The Writings
The Twelve
The Torah
Chronicles
check.why: Tradition and scholars agree the Torah came first; Nehemiah 8 describes Ezra reading it to the people around the 5th century BCE.

check.q: What does the phrase "make the hands unclean" mean in the rabbis' debates?
choices: The book is forbidden
The book was written in Greek
The book must be burned
The book is holy scripture
check.why: In the Mishnah, a book that "makes the hands unclean" is one treated as holy; the debates were about which books count as scripture.

check.q: How do most scholars today describe what happened at Yavneh?
choices: Discussions in a slow, informal process, not a single council that closed the canon
A formal vote that created the Torah
The writing of the book of Esther
The first translation into Greek
check.why: The older idea of a "Council of Jamnia" that closed the canon has been questioned; most scholars now see a gradual settling, with Yavneh as one moment in it.

lessons.title: Hebrew, Right to Left
lessons.mainIdea: Almost all of the Tanakh is written in Hebrew, read from right to left, in an alphabet of 22 letters that originally had no vowels.
reading: Open a Hebrew Bible and the first thing you notice is direction. *Hebrew* is read from right to left, so the book opens from what an English reader would call the back. The alphabet has 22 letters, and every one of them is a consonant. In the oldest texts there were no vowel marks at all.

Hebrew words are built on roots, usually three letters. The root K-T-V has to do with writing. From it come *ketuvim* (writings), *ketav* (script) and *katav* (he wrote). Once you know a root, you can spot a family of related words across the whole Tanakh.

Reading without vowels sounds hard, and sometimes it is. The three letters D-V-R can be read as davar, a word, or as dever, a plague, or as dibber, he spoke. Readers used context and tradition to know which was meant. Later, as you will see, scholars added marks to fix the reading.

Hebrew names in the Tanakh often carry meaning. Genesis says Isaac was named for laughter, and Moses for being drawn out of water. When a translation gives you only the sound of a name, the wordplay is lost. That is one reason many students of the Tanakh learn some Hebrew.

words.d: the language of almost all of the Tanakh; written right to left with 22 consonant letters
a set of usually three Hebrew letters that carries a core meaning shared by a family of words

look.title: The First Words in Hebrew and English

look.cite: Genesis 1:1, JPS Tanakh (1917); the Hebrew first word is Bereshit, "in the beginning," which gives the book its Hebrew name
look.prompt: The Hebrew verse has only seven words. Count the English words. What does a translator have to add to make Hebrew sound like English?

check.q: In which direction is Hebrew read?
choices: Left to right
Right to left
Top to bottom
Bottom to top
check.why: Hebrew, like Aramaic and Arabic, runs from right to left, so a Hebrew Bible opens from the side an English reader would call the back.

check.q: What is a Hebrew root?
choices: A vowel mark under a letter
The first word of a book
A set of about three letters that carries a core meaning shared by related words
A Greek translation of a Hebrew word
check.why: Hebrew words are built from roots; K-T-V, for example, gives ketuvim (writings) and katav (he wrote).

check.q: Why could the letters D-V-R be read in more than one way in an old Hebrew text?
choices: Hebrew has no consonants
The scribes wrote in code
D-V-R is a Greek word
The oldest texts had no vowel marks
check.why: Without vowels, the same consonants could be davar (word), dever (plague) or dibber (he spoke); readers relied on context and tradition.

lessons.title: Aramaic Pages and Targums
lessons.mainIdea: A few parts of the Tanakh are in Aramaic, a related language many Jews spoke after the exile, and later Aramaic translations called Targums helped listeners follow the Hebrew.
reading: Not every page of the Tanakh is Hebrew. About half of the book of Daniel is in *Aramaic*, from chapter 2 through chapter 7. So are parts of the book of Ezra, mostly letters to and from Persian kings. One verse of Jeremiah and two words in Genesis are Aramaic too.

Aramaic is a cousin of Hebrew. It uses the same alphabet and many similar words. In the centuries after the Babylonian exile, Aramaic was the everyday language across much of the Middle East. Many Jews spoke it at home and used Hebrew mainly for prayer and study.

That created a problem in the synagogue. The Torah was read in Hebrew, but not everyone understood it. So a translator would stand beside the reader and give each verse in Aramaic. These spoken translations were later written down. They are called *Targums*, from a word meaning translation.

The best known is Targum Onkelos on the Torah. It is more than a translation. Where the Hebrew says God's hand or God's anger, Onkelos often softens the picture, since Jewish tradition holds that God has no body. Reading a Targum shows you how ancient Jews understood the text, not just what it said.

words.d: a language close to Hebrew, widely spoken by Jews after the exile; parts of Daniel and Ezra are written in it
an ancient Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible, first spoken in the synagogue and later written down

look.title: Same Verse, Two Voices
look.text: Imagine a synagogue in Galilee around 200 CE. The reader chants a verse of Genesis in Hebrew. Then a second man, the meturgeman, repeats it in Aramaic so the farmers and traders in the room can follow. Where the Hebrew says God "went down" to see the tower of Babel, the Aramaic says God "revealed himself" to see it.
look.prompt: Why might the translator change "went down" to "revealed himself"? What does that choice tell you about what his listeners believed about God?

check.q: Which book of the Tanakh has the most Aramaic in it?
choices: Daniel
Genesis
Psalms
Isaiah
check.why: Daniel 2:4 through 7:28 is in Aramaic, about half the book; Ezra has Aramaic sections too, mostly official letters.

check.q: What is a Targum?
choices: A Hebrew commentary by Rashi
An Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible
A Greek translation made in Egypt
A scroll used only on Purim
check.why: Targums began as spoken Aramaic renderings in the synagogue so listeners who did not know Hebrew could follow; Targum Onkelos is the best known.

check.q: Why did synagogues need translators after the Babylonian exile?
choices: The Torah had been lost
Reading Hebrew aloud was forbidden
Many Jews spoke Aramaic every day and knew less Hebrew
The scrolls were written in Greek
check.why: Aramaic had become the everyday language across the region, so the Hebrew reading was followed by an Aramaic version verse by verse.

lessons.title: Adding the Vowels
lessons.mainIdea: Between about the 7th and 10th centuries CE, Jewish scholars called Masoretes added vowel points and accent marks so the text would be read the same way everywhere.
reading: For centuries the Hebrew Bible was copied with consonants only. The right way to read each word was passed down by teachers, mouth to ear. Then, between about the 7th and 10th centuries CE, scholars in Tiberias, by the Sea of Galilee, and in Babylonia set out to write that tradition down. They are called the *Masoretes*, from *masorah*, meaning what is handed on.

The Masoretes did not change the letters. Instead they added small dots and dashes under, above and inside them. These *vowel points* tell the reader which vowel to say. With them, D-V-R can only be read one way. The system used in Tiberias became the standard, and it is the one printed in Hebrew Bibles today.

They also added accent marks, called *te'amim*. These marks do three jobs at once. They show which syllable is stressed. They show how the verse breaks into phrases, like punctuation. And they tell the reader which musical notes to chant. You will learn more about that chanting later in the chapter.

The most respected Masoretic family was the Ben Asher family of Tiberias. Aaron ben Asher worked in the early 10th century. His text became the model for Jewish tradition and for later scholars. Maimonides, the great 12th-century scholar, wrote that he relied on a Ben Asher codex. He used it when writing his own Torah scroll.

words.d: Jewish scholars of about the 7th to 10th centuries CE who added vowels, accents and notes to the Hebrew text
small dots and dashes placed around Hebrew consonants to show which vowel sound to read
accent marks that show stress, phrasing and the melody for chanting a verse

look.title: Ways the Hebrew Text Was Marked, in Order
look.cite: Commonly cited dates: Ketef Hinnom amulets c. 7th century BCE; Great Isaiah Scroll c. 125 BCE; Aleppo Codex c. 930 CE; Soncino Hebrew Bible 1488
look.prompt: How many centuries passed between the oldest known biblical text and the vowel system used today? What kept the reading steady in between?

check.q: What did the Masoretes add to the Hebrew text?
choices: New chapters at the end of Chronicles
A Greek translation between the lines
Illustrations of each story
Vowel points, accents and notes, without changing the letters
check.why: The Masoretes marked the traditional reading with dots, dashes and accents; the consonants stayed as they were.

check.q: Where did the standard system of vowel points come from?
choices: Tiberias, by the Sea of Galilee
Alexandria in Egypt
Troyes in France
Rome
check.why: Several systems existed, but the Tiberian system, linked with the Ben Asher family, became the one printed in Hebrew Bibles today.

check.q: Which of these is NOT a job of the te'amim accent marks?
choices: Showing which syllable is stressed
Showing which vowel to say
Showing how a verse breaks into phrases
Showing the melody for chanting
check.why: Vowels are shown by the vowel points; the te'amim handle stress, phrasing and the chant melody.

lessons.title: Notes in the Margins
lessons.mainIdea: The masorah is a set of margin notes that count letters and words and flag unusual spellings, so copyists could catch any change.
reading: Look at a page from a Masoretic codex and you see more than the Bible text. Around the edges, in tiny letters, run notes. This is the *masorah*. It is a kind of security system for the text. The notes say things like: this word appears four times spelled this way, or this is the middle letter of the Torah.

The Masoretes counted everything. They counted the verses in each book. They counted the words. They noted the exact middle verse of the Torah, in Leviticus, and the middle word. Why? If a copy had the right counts, the copyist could trust that nothing had been added or dropped.

The notes also record places where the reading tradition and the written letters differ. The written form is called *ketiv*, what is written. The spoken form is called *qere*, what is read. The scribe keeps the ketiv in the text and puts the qere in the margin. The reader says the qere aloud. Neither one is erased.

Modern scholars find the masorah valuable for a different reason. Because the notes freeze a snapshot of the text as it stood around 900 CE, they let scholars check later copies against it. The notes were meant to guard the text for the community. They also became a tool for the historian.

words.d: the Masoretes' margin notes that count letters, words and verses and mark unusual readings
"written" and "read": a place where the text's letters and the traditional spoken reading differ, and both are kept

look.title: Why Count the Letters?
look.text: A Masoretic note beside Leviticus 8:8 says this is the middle verse of the Torah. Another note marks the middle word and another the middle letter. A modern editor might think this is odd. But picture a scribe in the year 1000 finishing a copy of the Torah with no printing press, no photocopy and no way to compare two texts side by side except by eye.
look.prompt: How could counting the middle verse, word and letter help that scribe know his copy was complete? What are the limits of that method?

check.q: What is the masorah?
choices: The Aramaic translation read in the synagogue
The list of 24 books
Margin notes that count and record features of the text to protect it from change
The melody used for chanting
check.why: The masorah is the set of notes the Masoretes wrote around the text, counting words and letters and marking unusual spellings.

check.q: In a ketiv-qere note, what does the reader say aloud?
choices: The ketiv, the written letters
Both, one after the other
Neither; the verse is skipped
The qere, the traditional reading
check.why: The ketiv stays in the text and the qere is written in the margin; the reader pronounces the qere.

check.q: Why did the Masoretes count the words and letters of each book?
choices: So a copyist could check that nothing had been added or dropped
To decide which books belong in the canon
To translate the text into Greek
To fix the order of the Writings
check.why: Matching counts showed a copy was complete; the masorah worked as a checking system for scribes.

lessons.title: Two Famous Codices
lessons.mainIdea: The Aleppo Codex (c. 930 CE) and the Leningrad Codex (1008 CE) are the oldest and most complete Masoretic Bibles, and printed Hebrew Bibles today are based on them.
reading: A scroll is long and hard to search. Around the 8th century, Jewish scribes began also copying the Bible into a *codex*, a book with pages. Scrolls stayed in use for the synagogue reading. Codices were for study, and they had room in the margins for the masorah.

The most famous is the *Aleppo Codex*, written in Tiberias around 930 CE. Tradition says Aaron ben Asher himself added its vowels and notes. Maimonides praised it. For about six hundred years it was kept in a synagogue in Aleppo, Syria. In 1947 the synagogue was attacked, and when the codex reached Israel in 1958 about a third of its pages were missing, including most of the Torah. What remains is in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

The *Leningrad Codex* was written in Cairo in 1008 CE, according to its own note. It is the oldest complete Masoretic Bible in the world. Since the 19th century it has been in the national library in St. Petersburg, Russia, which was called Leningrad for much of the 20th century. Most scholarly Hebrew Bibles today print its text.

Something surprising comes from comparing these codices with the Dead Sea Scrolls, which are about a thousand years older. The Great Isaiah Scroll from about 125 BCE matches the Masoretic Isaiah in nearly every word. There are small differences in spelling and a few in wording. But the text the Masoretes fixed was very close to what scribes had copied a thousand years before.

words.d: a handwritten book with pages, unlike a scroll; the plural is codices
a Masoretic Bible from Tiberias, c. 930 CE, long kept in Aleppo, Syria; part of it is now lost
a Masoretic Bible from 1008 CE, the oldest complete one; the base of most scholarly Hebrew Bibles
ancient manuscripts found near the Dead Sea from 1947 on, including Bible texts about a thousand years older than the Masoretic codices

look.title: Ages of Key Manuscripts
look.cite: Dates as given by the Israel Museum (Shrine of the Book) and the National Library of Russia
look.prompt: About how many years separate the Great Isaiah Scroll from the Aleppo Codex? Why does it matter that the two texts of Isaiah are so alike?

check.q: Which is the oldest complete Masoretic Bible?
choices: The Aleppo Codex
The Leningrad Codex
The Great Isaiah Scroll
The Septuagint
check.why: The Leningrad Codex of 1008 CE is complete; the older Aleppo Codex lost about a third of its pages after 1947.

check.q: What is a codex?
choices: A rolled scroll
A margin note
A handwritten book with pages
A vowel mark
check.why: A codex is a book form with pages, which gave scribes room to write the masorah around the text; the synagogue reading still uses a scroll.

check.q: What did scholars find when they compared the Great Isaiah Scroll with the Masoretic text of Isaiah?
choices: The scroll was a different book entirely
The scroll was written in Greek
The scroll had no vowels, so it could not be read
The two texts match in nearly every word, with small differences
check.why: Despite a gap of about a thousand years, the Isaiah scroll and the Masoretic Isaiah are very close, showing how stable the copying was.

lessons.title: How a Torah Scroll Is Made
lessons.mainIdea: A Torah scroll is handwritten by a trained scribe on parchment from a kosher animal, with a quill and special ink, following rules that have changed little in a thousand years.
reading: Every synagogue keeps at least one Torah scroll in a cabinet called the ark. The scroll is not printed. It is written by hand by a *sofer*, a scribe trained for years in the rules of the work. Jewish law lays out those rules in detail, and most go back to the Talmud and the centuries after it.

The writing surface is *parchment*, made from the skin of a kosher animal such as a cow, goat or deer. The sheets are sewn together with thread made from animal sinew. A full Torah has about sixty sheets and is roughly the length of a school hallway when unrolled. The ink is black and made from a traditional recipe.

The scribe writes with a quill, usually from a turkey or goose feather. Before beginning, the scribe scores faint lines into the parchment so the letters sit straight. Each letter is formed in a set way. Some letters carry small crowns, called *tagin*. The scribe must copy from a correct model and may not write from memory.

The numbers are large. Jewish tradition counts 304,805 letters in a Torah scroll, and about 5,845 verses. A scribe writing full time may take a year or more to finish one scroll. That is why a scroll is costly, and why a community treats a new one like a member of the family, dancing it into the synagogue.

words.d: a Jewish scribe trained to write Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot by hand according to Jewish law
writing material made from animal skin; a Torah scroll is written on parchment from a kosher animal
the cabinet at the front of a synagogue where the Torah scrolls are kept

look.title: A Torah Scroll by the Numbers
look.cite: Traditional counts as given in Jewish sources and by scribes; the verse count is often cited as 5,845
look.prompt: If a scribe writes about 1,000 letters a day, roughly how many days of writing does one scroll take? What else might slow the work down?

check.q: Who writes a Torah scroll?
choices: A trained scribe called a sofer, by hand
A printing press
The rabbi of the synagogue, from memory
A committee of translators
check.why: Torah scrolls are handwritten by a sofer who copies from a correct model according to Jewish law; they are never printed.

check.q: What is a Torah scroll written on?
choices: Papyrus from Egypt
Parchment from a kosher animal
Paper made from wood pulp
Thin sheets of copper
check.why: Jewish law requires parchment from a kosher animal, with the sheets sewn together with sinew thread.

check.q: About how many letters does a Torah scroll contain, by the traditional count?
check.why: Tradition counts 304,805 letters; 5,845 is the approximate verse count, 54 the weekly portions and 24 the books of the Tanakh.

lessons.title: Checking and Retiring a Scroll
lessons.mainIdea: A scroll with an error or damage is unfit for public reading until fixed, and worn-out scrolls are not thrown away but stored or buried with respect.
reading: When a scroll is finished, the work is not over. A second expert checks every column against a model text. Today many checkers also use a computer program that scans the scroll and flags any letter whose shape looks wrong. A missing letter, an extra letter, or two letters touching makes the scroll *pasul*, unfit for use in the synagogue service.

Most mistakes can be fixed. The scribe scrapes the dry ink from the parchment and writes the letter again. But one kind of error is different. If the scribe has written one of the names of God by mistake, it may not be erased. Jewish tradition treats the divine name as too holy to scrape away. The whole sheet must be set aside and replaced.

Scrolls wear out. Ink cracks and flakes, parchment tears. A scroll that can no longer be repaired is not thrown in the trash. Because it holds God's name, Jewish practice is to store it in a special room called a *genizah*, or to bury it in a cemetery with the same respect given to a person.

A genizah once gave historians a gift. In the 1890s, scholars opened the genizah of the Ben Ezra synagogue in Cairo and found hundreds of thousands of pages, some a thousand years old. They included Bible texts, letters, contracts and lost books. A room meant for retiring worn pages turned out to be a treasure house of Jewish history.

words.d: unfit; a Torah scroll with an error or damage that may not be used for the synagogue reading until fixed
a storage place for worn-out writings that contain God's name, kept there instead of being thrown away

look.title: A Scroll Is Not Trash
look.text: In a synagogue in Chicago, an old Torah scroll has cracked so badly it can no longer be read from. The congregation gathers at a cemetery. They wrap the scroll and bury it, and some people cry. A visitor asks why anyone would hold a funeral for a book.
look.prompt: How would a member of the congregation explain what they are doing and why? What does the practice say about how the community sees the words in the scroll?

check.q: What makes a Torah scroll pasul?
choices: Being more than ten years old
Having vowel points
Being written in Aramaic
An error or damage, such as a missing letter or two letters touching
check.why: Pasul means unfit: a scroll with any error or damage may not be used for the public reading until it is repaired.

check.q: Why can a mistake in writing God's name not be fixed by scraping?
choices: Jewish tradition holds the divine name too holy to erase, so the sheet is replaced
The ink used for the name is permanent
The scribe would have to start the whole scroll over
Scraping would tear the parchment
check.why: Ordinary letters are scraped and rewritten, but a written name of God may not be erased; that sheet is set aside.

check.q: What is a genizah?
choices: The cabinet that holds the Torah scrolls in use
A storage place for worn-out writings that contain God's name
A room where scribes are trained
A pointer used during the reading
check.why: A genizah holds writings too worn to use but too holy to throw away; the Cairo Genizah preserved a treasure of old pages.

lessons.title: Chanting the Text
lessons.mainIdea: The Tanakh is chanted, not just read, using melodies fixed by the te'amim, and the tunes differ by community and by the book being read.
reading: In the synagogue, the Torah is not read in a speaking voice. It is chanted. The reader follows the *te'amim*, the accent marks the Masoretes recorded. Each mark stands for a short musical phrase. Strung together, they turn a verse into a melody. English-speaking Jews often call this *trope*, and learning it is a big part of preparing for a bar or bat mitzvah.

The chanting does real work. Because the marks also show where phrases begin and end, the melody tells the listener how the sentence is built. A rising tune means more is coming. A falling tune means the thought is done. A careful reader can hear the grammar of a verse.

Here is the catch: the scroll itself has no marks at all. No vowels, no accents, no punctuation. The reader must learn the vowels and the melody from a printed book and then chant from the bare letters. A helper follows along and corrects any slip. That is why a reader practices for weeks.

The tunes are not the same everywhere. Jews whose families came from Germany and Eastern Europe, called *Ashkenazi*, use one set of melodies. Jews from Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, called *Sephardi* and Mizrahi, use others. And the same marks are sung to a different tune for the Torah, for the Prophets, and for Esther on Purim.

words.d: the traditional melody for chanting the Tanakh, fixed by the te'amim marks; also called cantillation
Jews whose families came from Germany and Eastern Europe, with their own customs and melodies
Jews whose families came from Spain and Portugal, and by extension many Mediterranean and Middle Eastern communities

look.title: Reading with Meaning
look.text: And they read in the book, in the Law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
look.cite: Nehemiah 8:8, closely following the JPS Tanakh (1917); the Talmud (Megillah 3a) reads this verse as describing translation, verse division and the accent marks
look.prompt: The verse says the readers "gave the sense." How could a melody that shows where phrases break help a listener understand a text?

check.q: What do the te'amim tell a Torah reader?
choices: Which book to read next
How to translate the verse into Aramaic
The melody and where the phrases of a verse begin and end
Which sheet of parchment to use
check.why: The te'amim mark stress, phrasing and the chant melody, so the tune carries the grammar of the verse.

check.q: Why is chanting from a Torah scroll harder than chanting from a printed book?
choices: The scroll is written in Greek
The letters in a scroll are much smaller
Scrolls may only be read at night
The scroll has no vowels or accent marks, so the reader must know them from memory
check.why: A scroll has bare consonants; the reader learns vowels and melody from a printed text and then chants from the unmarked letters.

check.q: How do Ashkenazi and Sephardi chanting differ?
choices: They sing the same marks to different melodies
Sephardi Jews do not chant at all
Ashkenazi Jews read the Torah in Yiddish
They use different Torah scrolls with different words
check.why: The te'amim are the same in every community, but the tunes attached to them vary by tradition and by the book being read.

review.q: Which list gives the three parts of the Tanakh in order?
choices: Ketuvim, Torah, Nevi'im
Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim
Torah, Talmud, Targum
Genesis, Psalms, Malachi
review.why: The Tanakh's three parts are Torah (Teaching), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings), in that order.

review.q: The Christian Old Testament ends with Malachi. What does the Tanakh end with?
choices: Deuteronomy, with the death of Moses
Psalm 150
Chronicles, with a call to go up to Jerusalem
Esther
review.why: Chronicles is the last book of the Writings, and its final verse is Cyrus's call to go up to Jerusalem.

review.q: Which statement about the Masoretes is correct?
choices: They translated the Torah into Greek in Alexandria
They wrote the book of Daniel in Aramaic
They were the first to print the Hebrew Bible
They added vowel points, accents and notes to the consonant text between about the 7th and 10th centuries CE
review.why: The Masoretes of Tiberias and Babylonia fixed the reading with marks and notes; they did not change the letters or translate.

review.q: What do the ketiv and the qere show?
choices: A place where the written letters and the traditional reading differ, and both are kept
Two different melodies for the same verse
The Hebrew and Aramaic versions of a verse
The first and last verses of a book
review.why: Ketiv means "written" and qere means "read"; the scribe keeps the letters and the margin gives the reading.

review.q: Why is the Leningrad Codex important to scholars?
choices: It is the only copy of the Torah written by Moses
It is the oldest complete Masoretic Bible, and most scholarly Hebrew Bibles print its text
It is the oldest Dead Sea Scroll
It is the first Bible printed by Bomberg
review.why: Written in 1008 CE, the Leningrad Codex is complete; the older Aleppo Codex lost many pages.

review.q: A student says the Tanakh is written entirely in Hebrew. What is the best correction?
choices: It is written entirely in Aramaic
It was written in Greek and translated into Hebrew later
Almost all of it is Hebrew, but parts of Daniel and Ezra are in Aramaic
Half of it is Hebrew and half is Latin
review.why: Aramaic appears in Daniel 2–7, parts of Ezra, one verse of Jeremiah and two words in Genesis; the rest is Hebrew.

review.q: Which rule applies to writing a Torah scroll?
choices: The scribe may print the text if the font is traditional
The scribe writes from memory to prove skill
The scroll must include vowel points
The scribe must copy from a correct model onto parchment from a kosher animal
review.why: Jewish law requires a trained sofer to copy by hand from a model onto kosher parchment; the scroll has no vowels or accents.

review.q: What did the comparison of the Great Isaiah Scroll with the Masoretic text show?
choices: The text of Isaiah stayed very stable over about a thousand years
The book of Isaiah was written after the Masoretes
The Masoretes rewrote most of Isaiah
The Dead Sea Scrolls were forgeries
review.why: The scroll from about 125 BCE and the Masoretic Isaiah agree in nearly every word, with small differences in spelling.
